source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: Across 83 independent samples from 64 studies, gesture with speech gave a medium benefit to comprehension versus speech alone.
numbers: Overall pooled d = .61, 95% CI .50-.72, z = 11.04. Total 3,883 participants (sample sizes 12-184). 80 of 83 effect sizes positive, but only 68% of samples were individually significant. Cochran Q = 265.60, I2 = 69.1%.
limits: Heterogeneity is high. Mostly comprehension of a message, not the gesturer's own problem solving. Only 1 of 83 studies had blinded staff.
agent_relevance: Background only: gesture helps people take in and hold content. No direct operator for a text-only agent.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: Producing gestures helped more than watching them. This is the core evidence for gesture as the gesturer's own thinking tool.
numbers: Production: 17 samples, d = .91 (CI .64-1.19, I2 72.1%). Observation: 66 samples, d = .54 (CI .43-.66, I2 67.3%). Production beat observation significantly in the meta-regression.
limits: Only 17 production samples. Tasks differ between production and observation studies, so the comparison is confounded by task.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the useful thing is the act, not the display. An LLM has no hands, so the analogue would be writing or drawing as an act, not reading.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: Gesture type did not significantly moderate the effect. Iconic, deictic, metaphoric and mixed gestures helped. Beat gestures did not clearly help.
numbers: Iconic d = .66 (CI .50-.82, k=28); deictic .43 (.25-.61, k=16); metaphoric 1.41 (.16-2.67, k=2); beat .20 (.03-.43, p = .093, k=2); mixed .42 (.17-.67, k=19). Meta-regression: no type differed significantly from beat.
limits: Only 2 samples each for beat and metaphoric. The beat null may be low power, as the authors say.
agent_relevance: Pointing (deictic) works about as well as depictive gestures. This hints that attention and anchoring may carry part of the effect.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: Age did not significantly moderate the effect. Adolescent samples were the one group with no significant benefit.
numbers: Preschool d = .73 (CI .49-.97); primary .58 (.42-.75); adolescent .68 (CI .07-1.41, ns, only 2 samples); adult .57 (.40-.74). Meta-regression ns at Bonferroni alpha .017.
limits: This contradicts Hostetter (2011), who found children benefit more. Adolescent cell has k = 2.
agent_relevance: Benefit does not vanish with maturity. No reason to expect a strong-model discount.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: The measure of comprehension changed the size of the effect, though not significantly in meta-regression. Free recall gave the largest effects, multiple choice the smallest.
numbers: Free recall d = .91 (CI .54-1.28, I2 87.5%, k=15); open or specific questions .55 (.45-.65, k=47); forced choice .47 (.19-.76, k=17); mixture .86 (.56-1.16, k=4).
limits: Free recall has huge heterogeneity (I2 87.5%).
agent_relevance: Suggests gesture helps generation and memory more than recognition. Fits a view of gesture as a retrieval and construction aid.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: Publication bias evidence is mixed. Egger's test was significant in some strata. Trim-and-fill added no studies overall.
numbers: Fail-safe N = 170. 15 Egger tests run, some significant. Two outliers (d = 1.07, 1.14) removed: overall mean stayed .63, I2 67.6%. Additional-information gestures d = .75 vs redundant .52 (not significantly different).
limits: Authors say effects may be overestimated in some strata.
agent_relevance: Treat d = .6 as an upper-ish estimate. Discount for bias.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: a meta-analysis of gesture and comprehension
finding: The earlier meta-analysis by Hostetter (2011) found nearly the same mean effect, so the headline number is stable across two meta-analyses.
numbers: Hostetter 2011: mean d = .61 over 63 samples (as reported in Dargue et al.). Dargue 2019: d = .61 over 83 samples.
limits: The second pool overlaps heavily with the first, so this is not fully independent confirmation. Hostetter 2011 itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Stable but modest, domain-general effect.

source: Kisa, Goldin-Meadow & Casasanto (2021) Do gestures really facilitate speech production?
finding: Failed conceptual replication of the lexical retrieval claim. Preventing gesture did not raise speech disfluency, even for literal spatial speech.
numbers: 56 subjects in pairs retold 6 stories (2 literal spatial, 4 metaphorical spatial); 12 stories; 7,969 phrases (4,000 gesture allowed, 3,969 prevented); 2,075 disfluencies. Overall disfluency rate prevented M = .07 vs allowed M = .06, chi2(1) = 1.07, p = .30. Spatial speech chi2(1) = 1.71, p = .19. Non-spatial chi2(1) = .56, p = .45.
quote: no reliable evidence that preventing gestures makes speech more disfluent
limits: Gesture prevention was by holding down keys. Null results do not prove absence. Trends went opposite to the lexical retrieval prediction. Conference paper.
agent_relevance: Weakens the claim that gesture mainly helps find words. Keep any gesture-based scaffold claim tied to spatial and working memory roles instead.

source: Kisa, Goldin-Meadow & Casasanto (2021) Do gestures really facilitate speech production?
finding: Re-examination of the founding study (Rauscher, Krauss & Chen 1996) found its key interaction was never tested and its stats were liberal.
numbers: Literal spatial disfluency: chi2(1) = .97, p = .32. Metaphorical with spatial language chi2(1) = 1.56, p = .21; without spatial language chi2(1) = 1.09, p = .30. Gesture x content interaction chi2(1) = .30, p = .58. In the gesture-allowed arm, 2,249 gestures were produced (1,609 beats, 328 iconic).
limits: The authors judge the original tests ignored item variance and did not correct for multiple comparisons. This is the authors' reanalysis, not a direct replication of the 1996 design.
agent_relevance: A caution against building on a single classic study. Treat the lexical retrieval account as unsupported.

source: Cook, Yip & Goldin-Meadow (2012) Gestures, but not meaningless movements, lighten working memory load when explaining math
finding: Meaningful gesture reduced working memory load. Meaningless movement or no movement did not. This separates a meaning account from a mere motor or rhythm account.
numbers: N = 115 college students; 30 polynomial factoring problems plus letter-recall load. Letter recall lower with Meaningless Movement (beta = -.17, z = 3.23, p < .01) and No Movement (beta = -.13, z = 2.61, p < .01) than with gesturing. First-condition-only between-subject check: Meaningless beta = -.30, p = .057; No Movement beta = -.36, p = .02.
limits: Between-subject check was only marginal for meaningless movement. Gestures were mostly pointing sequences. Adults, one task type.
agent_relevance: Strongest discriminating experiment against rhythm accounts. Offloading helps only when the movement carries task content, like a scratchpad that matches the problem.

source: Cook, Yip & Goldin-Meadow (2012) Gestures, but not meaningless movements, lighten working memory load when explaining math
finding: Easier word finding did not explain the memory benefit. Meaningless movement gave fewer filled pauses, yet gave no memory gain.
numbers: Estimated probability of a non-juncture filled pause: Meaningful .24, No Movement .26, Meaningless .16 (beta = -.56, z = 2.62, p < .01). Words per explanation: 46.9, 46.3, 52.8 (Meaningless vs Meaningful beta = 5.9, p MCMC < .01). No reliable effect on speech rate.
limits: Speech measures checked on two groups only. Adults.
agent_relevance: Another piece of evidence against the lexical retrieval account, from a different lab than Kisa et al. The benefit tracks meaning, not word access.

source: Cook, Yip & Goldin-Meadow (2010) Gesturing makes memories that last
finding: Gesturing during encoding improved memory, mainly after delay and on free recall. The abstract states it held whether gesture was spontaneous or instructed.
numbers: Study 1: N = 17 undergraduates (10 returned at about 3 weeks); 26 animated vignettes; speakers gestured on 47% (SD 36%) of vignettes. Gesture x Delay beta = .36, z = 2.7, p = .007; Gesture x Test beta = .27, z = 2.2, p = .03; main effect of Gesture ns.
limits: Very small N in Study 1. Spontaneous gesture is not randomly assigned. Memory for motion vignettes, not reasoning. Study 2 (instructed) statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Suggests writing out and acting out task content may aid retention. Weak, small-sample base.

source: The role of motor context in the beneficial effects of hand gesture on memory (PMC6824968)
finding: Replicated an earlier result (Iani & Bucciarelli) that an unrelated motor task at encoding or at retrieval removes the memory benefit of seeing gesture. A new condition showed matching motor context at both stages restores it. This is a boundary condition on motor-engagement accounts.
numbers: Mean 5.70 of 12 phrases recalled (SD 1.75). Best cell: no tapping, gesture seen (M = 7.00). Worst: tapping at both stages, no gesture (M = 5.05). Literal recall 4.31, paraphrase 1.38 per set. The first omnibus model showed no significant interactions.
limits: Observing gesture, not producing it. Memory for phrases, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: The 'busy hands kill the effect' result is partly context mismatch, so it is not a clean mechanism test.

source: Kersey et al. (2024) The effects of gesture and action training on the retention of math equivalence
finding: Children learned from both gesture and action, but only gesture-trained children improved over four weeks. Action-trained children held steady.
numbers: Study 1: 71 children (about 36 per arm) of 142 total across both studies. Immediate proportion correct: action .47, gesture .53; next day action .49, gesture .54. Trained Form A .70 vs untrained forms B .42 and C .41. Gesture training: time chi2(1) = 11.23, p = .0008; action training: time chi2(1) = 1.83, p = .176.
limits: Raw differences at immediate test are small; the claim rests on a condition x time interaction. One math concept, one lab.
agent_relevance: Gesture helps retention more than first learning. For an agent, durable summaries may matter more than immediate enactment.

source: Kersey et al. (2024) The effects of gesture and action training on the retention of math equivalence
finding: Training order mattered by prior knowledge. Children with few strategies did better with action before gesture. Children with many strategies did equally well in either order.
numbers: Study 2: action-then-gesture n = 36, gesture-then-action n = 35. Four-week proportion correct AG .57, GA .48. Condition x time chi2(1) = 12.38, p = .0004. Study 1 pretest: mismatchers conveyed 3.50 (SD .95) unique strategies vs 2.00 (SD .69) for non-mismatchers.
limits: Moderator is spontaneous gesture-speech mismatch at pretest, a coarse split. Study 2 has no gesture-only control.
agent_relevance: Individual differences moderate: concrete then abstract for novices. Matches fading from external to internal.

source: Pouw, de Nooijer, van Gog, Zwaan & Paas (2014) Toward a more embedded/extended perspective on the cognitive function of gestures
finding: Proposes gestures are external tools that replace or support internal processes, not only outputs of motor simulation. Reviews moderators of gesture use.
numbers: Review, no new data. Cited cases: people with low working memory capacity are hurt more when barred from gesturing (Marstaller & Burianova 2013); children aged 2-4 point more under memory demand (Delgado et al. 2011).
quote: gestures are external physical tools of the cognitive system that replace and support otherwise solely internal cognitive processes
limits: Mostly theory. Authors admit gestures can hinder performance or learning in some settings (De Nooijer; Post et al. 2013). Cited numbers not given.
agent_relevance: Supports the tool framing. Predicts offloading helps most when internal capacity is low or the task is hard.

source: Pouw, de Nooijer, van Gog, Zwaan & Paas (2014) Toward a more embedded/extended perspective on the cognitive function of gestures
finding: Gesture use fades with practice. This is a boundary condition tied to expertise and familiarity.
numbers: Chu & Kita (2008) as cited: in mental rotation, gestures move from as-if manipulation to a stand-in rotating flat hand, then disappear. Abacus experts gesture less as they improve.
limits: Secondhand summary of cited work; numbers not given.
agent_relevance: A scaffold should fade with competence. Do not force the external step on easy items.

source: Chu & Kita (2011) The nature of gestures' beneficial role in spatial problem solving (from a search summary)
finding: Encouraging gesture improved mental rotation, and the advantage carried into later gesture-free spatial problems. Key evidence that gesture changes internal computation.
numbers: Experiment 2: 66 participants, gesture-encouraged beat gesture-allowed and gesture-prohibited groups; Experiment 3: 32 participants. Exact group means not read.
limits: PDF could not be opened (the download returned a block page), so numbers come from a search summary. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Training on external manipulation transfers to internal use, a candidate for worked examples.

source: Wheeler (2013) Is cognition embedded or extended? The case of gestures (chapter in The Hand, an Organ of the Mind, MIT Press)
finding: Philosophical rival-theory test: the gesture evidence supports a conservative embedded view, not extended cognition. Gestures help thinking but are not themselves part of thinking.
numbers: Reviews Goldin-Meadow et al. 2001 (matched child groups; gesturers recalled more of a memorised list after a math task), Broaders et al. 2007 (children told to gesture revealed unspoken strategies and learned more from the later lesson), Hutchins 2010 (instructor pilot gesture).
quote: gestures help us to think, but (in the relevant sense) they are not themselves part of thinking
limits: Philosophy chapter; no new data. The cited experiments are described without numbers.
agent_relevance: Even if gestures are real cognitive helpers, they can be treated as a scaffold, as a phone is for storing numbers. Safe framing for the agent.

source: Wheeler (2013) Is cognition embedded or extended? The case of gestures (chapter in The Hand, an Organ of the Mind, MIT Press)
finding: Wheeler lists three deflationary readings that the data cannot rule out: offloading without cognitive status, gestures as windows on neural strategy, and tool-like props.
numbers: Quotes Clark: all the cognitive benefits of gesture may be secured by a covert, fully neural route. The experiments cannot separate covert neural from gesture-realised cognition.
limits: Argument, not data.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations remain open. Do not claim embodiment is needed for a text agent.

source: Iconic hand gestures and divergent creative thinking (Psychological Research 2024, PMC11142943)
finding: Encouraging gesture did not clearly raise average divergent thinking scores. Individual iconic gesture frequency predicted some measures.
numbers: N = 80 young adults (Group 1 n = 40 both conditions; Group 2 n = 40 encouraged only). Alternative Uses Task means: fluency 6.09 spontaneous vs 5.90 encouraged (Group 1) vs 5.63 (Group 2); originality 2.48, 2.49, 2.44; flexibility 4.31, 4.06, 3.63; elaboration 5.94, 7.09, 5.26. Iconic gesture rate 0.08, 0.13, 0.09.
limits: Predictors are correlational within condition. Gesture frequency negatively predicted flexibility in the spontaneous condition. Turkish-speaking sample. Only the descriptive means were read, not every model coefficient.
agent_relevance: Prior work found fluency gains in children and younger adults (as cited); this adult sample shows no clear mean shift. A boundary on creativity claims.

source: Iconic hand gestures and divergent creative thinking (Psychological Research 2024, PMC11142943)
finding: Mental imagery skill did not moderate gesture effects on divergent thinking.
numbers: Imagery measured with an 8-task battery (Di Nuovo et al. 2014); no gesture x imagery interaction reported in the abstract.
limits: One sample and one battery.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in imagery may matter less than predicted.

source: EcoG-Bench (arXiv 2603.07966, 2026) Can multimodal LLMs bind speech to co-speech pointing gestures?
finding: Frontier multimodal LLMs fail to bind spoken words to pointing gestures, while humans nearly ace it.
numbers: 811 bilingual egocentric clips. Human strict Eco-Accuracy 96.9%. Gemini-3-Pro 17.0% strict (63.9% classification); Gemini-3-Flash 7.0%; Qwen3-VL-30B 11.4%; GPT-5-mini 3.3%; Qwen3-Omni-30B 0.7%. Level 1 Gemini-3-Pro 30.2%; levels 3 and 4 fall to 10.6% and 10.2%, sequence success 1.8% and 0.4%.
limits: Tests perceiving gestures, not using them to think. Preprint, author list looked unfinished.
agent_relevance: Shows LLMs lack gesture-speech grounding. Nothing here tests gesture as a thinking aid.

source: EcoG-Bench (arXiv 2603.07966, 2026)
finding: Giving structured scaffolding (frames plus transcript) lifted strict gesture grounding sharply. This is a measured scaffold effect.
numbers: Gemini-3-Pro strict accuracy 17.0% to 42.9% (+25.9 points); sequence 10.9% to 25.5%. Gemini-3-Flash 7.0% to 48.1% (+41.1); sequence 4.1% to 30.8%. Qwen3-Omni-Flash 0.7% to 9.3%.
limits: Authors call the ablation a diagnostic probe that is not information-matched. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Rare AI-side evidence that structuring the input beats raw input. Supports a schema-style approach, in a perception task.

source: Li et al. (2025) Gestura: an LVLM system for free-form gesture understanding (IMWUT 9(4))
finding: A vision-language model with hand-landmark input and chain-of-thought reasoning beat the previous LLM gesture system at reading gesture intent.
numbers: Exocentric closed-set 84.73%, open-set 64.14%; egocentric closed-set 66.14%, open-set 21.71%. GestureGPT 72.08% (exocentric closed-set). Over 300,000 QA pairs. 1.6 s vs 227 s per query.
limits: Gesture recognition for human-computer interaction, not gesture as thought. Annotation and scoring used GPT-4o, so the judge is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought helps with ambiguous gestures. Weak link to our agent.

source: Torshizi, Hensel, Shapiro & Marsella (2025) Large language models for virtual human gesture selection (AAMAS)
finding: GPT-4 picks more appropriate gestures when prompted with a defined set of gestural intents than with no guidance. Two experts rated the output.
numbers: Four prompt approaches (0 none to 3 fullest); expert disagreement was very little. Approaches with a defined intent set gave more appropriate gestures and fewer inappropriate ones. Numeric rates not extracted.
limits: Gesture generation for avatars, not LLM thinking. Few annotated segments.
agent_relevance: Prompt structure matters for gesture reasoning. No test of gesture aiding reasoning.

source: Search sweep for LLM studies of gesture as a thinking aid (arXiv, Europe PMC, web search, 2020-2026)
finding: No LLM or AI study found that tests whether gesture-like external acts improve model reasoning. All found work is about recognising or generating gestures.
numbers: Found: EcoG-Bench, Gestura, Torshizi et al., Wicke (arXiv 2401.17858, a proposal for probing gesture understanding in text), FoMER and OmniEAR (embodied reasoning, not gesture). Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited, so the sweep is partial.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search.
agent_relevance: A real gap. The closest analogue is scratchpad or diagram writing, covered in other subfields.

source: Hostetter & Alibali (2019) Gesture as simulated action: revisiting the framework (search summary only)
finding: Framework review says evidence largely supports six predictions: gesture rate rises with simulation, with form, and with the cost of inhibiting gesture. It also reviews challenges.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only an abstract-level summary was seen. It is the rival to the tool view of Pouw et al.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: gestures may be motor spillover. A tool-use claim needs experiments that separate the two.
